lead: An ideal air-standard cycle replaces combustion with heat addition from an external source and uses air as the working fluid. It exists to compare engine cycles on equal terms: same air mass, ideal gas, constant specific heats, closed cycle, no intake or exhaust. The Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume; the Diesel cycle adds it at constant pressure; the dual cycle does both. Engineers use these cycles to see how compression ratio, cut-off ratio and heat input set efficiency and mean effective pressure before real losses enter. See Chapter 1.4 for the real SI and CI processes.
prereq: You need: ideal-gas relations and the first law from thermodynamics; Chapter 1.4 for the real SI and CI working principles.

blocks.text: An air-standard cycle treats the cylinder as a closed system filled with a fixed mass of air. Combustion is replaced by heat Q<sub>in</sub> added from an external source. Exhaust is replaced by heat Q<sub>out</sub> rejected to a sink. The same air returns to the starting state each cycle.

items: Air is an ideal gas: pV = mRT.
Specific heats c<sub>p</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> are constant, so γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> is constant. For air, γ = 1.4.
No intake or exhaust stroke, so no gas exchange.
No friction, no heat loss to walls, no chemical change.

blocks.text: These assumptions remove fuel chemistry, variable specific heats and heat transfer. That makes the Otto, Diesel and dual cycles comparable at the same compression ratio r and the same heat input Qin. The price is that air-standard efficiency is higher than a real engine's. Fuel-air cycles and actual losses are in Chapter 1.8.

sections.h3: Otto cycle: heat at constant volume

blocks.text: The Otto cycle has four processes:

items: 1–2: isentropic compression from V<sub>1</sub> to V<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.where: r = V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub> is the compression ratio; γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> is the specific heat ratio (1.4 for air); η<sub>Otto</sub> is thermal efficiency.

blocks.text: The formula contains no Q<sub>in</sub> and no temperature. For fixed γ, only r sets efficiency. Higher r raises efficiency. In a real SI engine, knock limits r; see Unit 3, Combustion in SI and CI Engines. Some syllabi call this the constant-volume cycle.

sections.h3: Diesel cycle: heat at constant pressure

blocks.text: The Diesel cycle replaces the constant-volume heat addition by constant-pressure heat addition. The piston moves while heat enters, so the volume grows from V<sub>2</sub> to V<sub>3</sub>. The cut-off ratio is ρ = V<sub>3</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>. A Diesel cycle has ρ > 1.

blocks.where: r is the compression ratio; ρ is the cut-off ratio; γ = 1.4 for air; η<sub>Diesel</sub> is thermal efficiency.

blocks.text: For ρ > 1 the bracket ((ρ<sup>γ</sup> − 1)/(γ(ρ − 1))) is greater than 1. So at the same r, Diesel efficiency is lower than Otto efficiency. Some syllabi call this the constant-pressure cycle.

sections.h3: Dual cycle, comparison and mean effective pressure

blocks.text: The dual cycle adds heat in two steps: first at constant volume, then at constant pressure. It uses a pressure ratio α = p<sub>3</sub>/p<sub>2</sub> and a cut-off ratio ρ = V<sub>4</sub>/V<sub>3</sub>. Otto and Diesel are special cases: α = 1 gives the Diesel cycle; ρ = 1 gives the Otto cycle.

blocks.where: α is the pressure ratio; ρ is the cut-off ratio; γ = 1.4 for air; r is the compression ratio.

blocks.text: For the same r and same Q<sub>in</sub>, the efficiency order is Otto > dual > Diesel. Mean effective pressure compares engines of different size:
MEP = W<sub>net</sub> / V<sub>s</sub>, with V<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: W<sub>net</sub> is net work per cycle in J; V<sub>s</sub> is swept volume in m<sup>3</sup>; MEP is in Pa (1 kPa = 10<sup>3</sup> Pa).

blocks.text: A high MEP means more work from a smaller engine. See Unit 5, Engine Testing and Performance for measured MEP.

figure.caption: Efficiency against compression ratio for Otto and Diesel cycles with γ = 1.4; the Diesel curve uses ρ = 2 and is valid only for r > ρ, so the plot starts at r = 2. At r = 8 the gap is 56.5% − 49.0% = 7.5 percentage points.

spec.aria: A plot compares Otto and Diesel efficiency against compression ratio starting at r = 2; Diesel uses a cut-off ratio of 2 and is valid only for r > ρ.

examples.question: An Otto cycle has compression ratio 8 and γ = 1.4. A Diesel cycle has the same compression ratio and cut-off ratio 2. Find both thermal efficiencies.
steps: Both cycles use r = 8 and γ = 1.4; the Diesel cycle also uses ρ = 2.
examples.answer: Otto efficiency is 56.5%; Diesel efficiency is 49.0% at the same compression ratio.
examples.check:
import math
r = 8.0
rho = 2.0
gamma = 1.4
eta_otto = 1 - 1/(r**(gamma-1))
eta_diesel = 1 - (1/(r**(gamma-1)))*((rho**gamma - 1)/(gamma*(rho-1)))
print(f"{eta_otto*100:.1f}")
print(f"{eta_diesel*100:.1f}")

traps: Diesel efficiency needs the cut-off ratio ρ; the Otto formula does not apply to a Diesel cycle.
At the same compression ratio, Otto is more efficient than Diesel. Do not compare at different r and claim a general rule.

For the Diesel cycle the cut-off ratio is ρ = V<sub>3</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>; for the dual cycle the numbering shifts and it is ρ = V<sub>4</sub>/V<sub>3</sub>. It is never the compression ratio r, and it equals 1 only in the Otto cycle.
MEP uses net work per cycle divided by swept volume; using piston displacement in litres without converting gives wrong units.
Air-standard efficiency is not brake efficiency; it ignores friction, heat loss and gas exchange (Chapter 1.8, Unit 5).

quiz.a: Fixed air mass and closed cycle; air is an ideal gas; constant specific heats with γ = 1.4; no intake, exhaust, friction or heat loss.

quiz.q: Which ideal cycle adds heat at constant volume, and which adds heat at constant pressure?
quiz.a: Otto adds heat at constant volume; Diesel adds heat at constant pressure.

quiz.q: Why does an air-standard cycle replace combustion with heat addition?
quiz.a: To remove fuel chemistry and compare cycles on the same thermodynamic basis. Heat addition gives the same energy input without modelling the fuel-air mixture and chemical reaction.

quiz.q: An Otto cycle has r = 10 and γ = 1.4. Find its thermal efficiency.
A Diesel cycle has r = 16, ρ = 2 and γ = 1.4. Find its thermal efficiency.
For the same compression ratio and same heat input, rank Otto, dual and Diesel efficiencies. Give one reason.
quiz.a: Otto > dual > Diesel. Diesel adds heat at constant pressure while the piston moves, so the cut-off factor is greater than 1 and efficiency is lower.

quiz.q: Why is a real SI engine's efficiency lower than the air-standard Otto value? Give three reasons.
quiz.a: Heat loss to walls; friction and pumping losses; gas exchange not ideal; variable specific heats and incomplete combustion also reduce efficiency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite-time thermodynamics adds finite piston speed and heat-transfer time to these cycles. Modern engine simulation uses variable specific heats and chemical equilibrium instead of a constant γ. Low-temperature combustion research (HCCI, RCCI) still uses air-standard cycles as a first estimate. Search next: dual cycle efficiency, finite-time Otto cycle, mean effective pressure.
